title: Causal Masking in Transformer Decoder
body:
The decoder computes attention scores for each query token against all key tokens. To prevent using future information, a causal mask adds $-\,\infty$ to any score where the key index $j$ exceeds the query index $i$.

```rh-diagram
{"version":1,"diagram":{"kind":"heatmap","title":"Causal mask before softmax","caption":"Gray cells are blocked (‑∞) so later keys get zero weight.","rowLabel":"Query position","columnLabel":"Key position","columns":["1","2","3","4","5","6"],"rows":[{"label":"1","cells":[null,null,null,null,null,null]},{"label":"2","cells":[0,null,null,null,null,null]},{"label":"3","cells":[0,0,null,null,null,null]},{"label":"4","cells":[0,0,0,null,null,null]},{"label":"5","cells":[0,0,0,0,null,null]},{"label":"6","cells":[0,0,0,0,0,null]}],"range":{"min":0,"max":1}}}
```

After adding the mask, the softmax normalises only the allowed scores, yielding a probability distribution that sums to 1 for each row. Consequently, each token can attend only to itself and earlier tokens.

The mask is a binary matrix: entry $(i,j)$ is 0 (allowed) when $j\le i$ and $-\infty$ (blocked) otherwise. This simple rule enforces the autoregressive property required for language generation.

title: Computing Gini Impurity and Information Gain
body:
Consider a parent node with four items of class 0 and four items of class 1, giving an initial impurity of $0.5$.

A split divides them into a left child with four items of class 0 and a right child with one item of class 0 and three of class 1.

```rh-diagram
{"version":1,"diagram":{"title":"Gini after the root split","caption":"Worked example. Combine the child Ginis in proportion to their sizes.","kind":"matrix","columns":["Class 0","Class 1","Gini","Weight"],"rows":[{"heading":"Left","cells":["4","0","0","0.5"]},{"heading":"Right","cells":["1","3","0.375","0.5"]},{"heading":"After","cells":["—","—","0.1875","1"]}]}}
```

For each child node, the Gini impurity is $1 - \sum p_i^2$, where $p_i$ is the fraction of each class. The left child has $1 - (1^2 + 0^2) = 0$, while the right child has $1 - (0.25^2 + 0.75^2) = 0.375$.

To find the combined impurity after the split, compute the weighted average of the child impurities based on their sizes. Here, both children have equal weight, yielding $0.5 \times 0 + 0.5 \times 0.375 = 0.1875$.

title: Computing Gini Impurity and Gain
body:
When a decision tree splits data, it evaluates how well the split separates classes by measuring the impurity reduction, known as information gain.

```rh-diagram
{"version":1,"diagram":{"title":"Gini after the root split","caption":"Worked example. Combine child Ginis in proportion to their sizes.","kind":"matrix","columns":["Class 0","Class 1","Gini","Weight"],"rows":[{"heading":"Left","cells":["4","0","0","0.5"]},{"heading":"Right","cells":["1","3","0.375","0.5"]},{"heading":"After","cells":["—","—","0.1875","1"]}]}}
```

To compute Gini impurity for any node, subtract the sum of squared class probabilities from one, using the formula $1 - \sum p_i^2$.

For the left child with four items of class zero and zero of class one, the impurity is zero because $1 - (1^2 + 0^2) = 0$.

For the right child with one class zero and three class ones, the impurity is $1 - (0.25^2 + 0.75^2) = 0.375$.

Information gain is then the parent impurity minus the weighted average of the child impurities, giving the net quality of the split.

body:
When building a decision tree, splitting nodes requires measuring how mixed the classes remain. Gini impurity measures the probability of misclassifying a randomly chosen element from a set.

Information gain is the reduction in impurity achieved by splitting the parent node. Subtract the weighted average of the child impurities from the parent impurity to find the total gain.

title: Stack vs Queue: How They Store and Retrieve
body:
A stack stores items in a linear list where the newest entry sits on top. When you push, the item becomes the new top; when you pop, the top item is removed first.

```rh-diagram

```

Thus a stack follows a LIFO (last‑in, first‑out) policy: the most recent element leaves before earlier ones.

```rh-diagram
{"version":1,"diagram":{"title":"Queue structure","caption":"Front on the left; first‑in, first‑out removal","kind":"layers","layers":[{"label":"Front element (oldest)"},{"label":"Middle element"},{"label":"Rear element (newest)"}]}}
```

A queue also uses a linear list, but new items join at the rear while removal happens at the front. Enqueue adds to the back; dequeue removes the front item.

The queue therefore obeys FIFO (first‑in, first‑out): the earliest element exits before later ones.

Both structures support constant‑time insertion and removal, yet their access order differs, making stacks ideal for backtracking and queues suited for task scheduling.
